```{python}
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
from sklearn.model_selection import KFold
from sklearn.linear_model import LassoCV
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
import patsy

# --- Airbnb Hackney case study ---
# Source: Bekes & Kezdi's public airbnb dataset, osf.io/qyca8, filtered to the Hackney
# borough workfile and matched to their published N=4,393 case study sample.
# GitHub raw URL (once pushed to the student data repo):
# air_df = pd.read_csv("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/stevenolanecon/7002LBSAI/main/data/airbnb_hackney.csv")
air_df = pd.read_csv("data/airbnb_hackney.csv")
air_df = air_df.loc[:, ~air_df.columns.duplicated()]
amenity_cols = [c for c in air_df.columns if c.startswith("d_")]
air_df["n_accommodates2"] = air_df["n_accommodates"] ** 2
air_df["n_days_since2"] = air_df["n_days_since"] ** 2

# --- The holdout split happens FIRST, before any model building, matching
# Gabor & Kezdi's own Ch.14 workflow (their case: 4,393 -> 3,515 work / 878
# holdout, roughly 80/20). Everything else in this file — the six models,
# cross-validation, BIC, LASSO, the bootstrap check — runs on work_df only.
# holdout_df is never touched until the very last diagnostic.
_rng = np.random.RandomState(20260921)
_holdout_mask = _rng.rand(len(air_df)) < 0.2
work_df = air_df.loc[~_holdout_mask].copy()
holdout_df = air_df.loc[_holdout_mask].copy()
n_work, n_holdout = len(work_df), len(holdout_df)

air_formulas = {
    "M1": "price ~ n_accommodates",
    "M2": "price ~ n_accommodates + n_beds + C(f_room_type) + C(f_property_type)",
    "M3": "price ~ n_accommodates + n_beds + C(f_room_type) + C(f_property_type) + n_bathrooms + C(f_cancellation_policy) + C(f_bed_type)",
    "M4": "price ~ n_accommodates + n_accommodates2 + n_beds + C(f_room_type) + C(f_property_type) + n_bathrooms + C(f_cancellation_policy) + C(f_bed_type) + n_days_since + n_days_since2",
    "M5": "price ~ n_accommodates + n_accommodates2 + n_beds + C(f_room_type)*C(f_property_type) + n_bathrooms + C(f_cancellation_policy) + C(f_bed_type) + n_days_since + n_days_since2",
}
air_formulas["M6"] = air_formulas["M5"] + " + " + " + ".join(amenity_cols)

air_fitted = {name: smf.ols(f, data=work_df).fit() for name, f in air_formulas.items()}

def _rmse(m):
    return float(np.sqrt(np.mean(m.resid ** 2)))

air_kf = KFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=20260921)
air_cv = {name: [] for name in air_formulas}
for tr_idx, te_idx in air_kf.split(work_df):
    train, test = work_df.iloc[tr_idx], work_df.iloc[te_idx]
    for name, f in air_formulas.items():
        m = smf.ols(f, data=train).fit()
        pred = m.predict(test)
        air_cv[name].append(float(np.sqrt(np.mean((test["price"] - pred) ** 2))))
air_cv_avg = {name: float(np.mean(v)) for name, v in air_cv.items()}

# --- Label engineering: log price needs a correction term to convert back.
# Fitted on work_df, same right-hand side as M6, so it's directly comparable
# to the level-price M6 already built above.
air_log_formula = air_formulas["M6"].replace("price ~", "np.log(price) ~")
log_m6 = smf.ols(air_log_formula, data=work_df).fit()
sigma_hat = float(np.sqrt(log_m6.mse_resid))
log_pred_work = log_m6.predict(work_df)
naive_pred_work = np.exp(log_pred_work)
corrected_pred_work = naive_pred_work * np.exp(sigma_hat ** 2 / 2)
label_actual_mean = float(work_df["price"].mean())
label_naive_mean = float(naive_pred_work.mean())
label_corrected_mean = float(corrected_pred_work.mean())

# One concrete listing, walked through step by step
_ex = work_df.iloc[0]
label_example = {
    "accommodates": int(_ex["n_accommodates"]),
    "room_type": str(_ex["f_room_type"]),
    "actual": float(_ex["price"]),
    "ln_pred": float(log_pred_work.iloc[0]),
    "naive": float(naive_pred_work.iloc[0]),
    "corrected": float(corrected_pred_work.iloc[0]),
}

air_stats_rows = [
    {"Model": name, "N coef": len(air_fitted[name].params), "R2": round(air_fitted[name].rsquared, 2),
     "Training RMSE": round(_rmse(air_fitted[name]), 1), "CV RMSE": round(air_cv_avg[name], 1),
     "BIC": int(round(air_fitted[name].bic))}
    for name in air_formulas
]

air_complexity_data = []
for name in air_formulas:
    ncoef = len(air_fitted[name].params)
    air_complexity_data.append({"n_coef": ncoef, "rmse": round(_rmse(air_fitted[name]), 1), "series": "Training RMSE", "model": name})
    air_complexity_data.append({"n_coef": ncoef, "rmse": round(air_cv_avg[name], 1), "series": "Cross-validated RMSE", "model": name})

# --- LASSO on the M6 feature set, fit on work_df only ---
y, X = patsy.dmatrices(air_formulas["M6"], data=work_df, return_type="dataframe")
y = y.values.ravel()
X = X.drop(columns=["Intercept"])
scaler = StandardScaler()
Xs = scaler.fit_transform(X)
lasso = LassoCV(cv=5, random_state=20260921, max_iter=20000).fit(Xs, y)
lasso_pred = lasso.predict(Xs)
lasso_rmse = float(np.sqrt(np.mean((y - lasso_pred) ** 2)))
n_nonzero = int(np.sum(lasso.coef_ != 0))
n_total = len(lasso.coef_)

lasso_kf = KFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=20260921)
lasso_cv_rmses = []
for tr_idx, te_idx in lasso_kf.split(Xs):
    lm = LassoCV(cv=5, random_state=20260921, max_iter=20000).fit(Xs[tr_idx], y[tr_idx])
    pred = lm.predict(Xs[te_idx])
    lasso_cv_rmses.append(float(np.sqrt(np.mean((y[te_idx] - pred) ** 2))))
lasso_cv_rmse = float(np.mean(lasso_cv_rmses))

def _nice(c):
    import re
    c = re.sub(r"C\(f_room_type\)\[T\.([^\]]+)\]", r"Room type: \1", c)
    c = re.sub(r"C\(f_property_type\)\[T\.([^\]]+)\]", r"Property type: \1", c)
    c = re.sub(r"C\(f_cancellation_policy\)\[T\.([^\]]+)\]", r"Cancellation: \1", c)
    c = re.sub(r"C\(f_bed_type\)\[T\.([^\]]+)\]", r"Bed type: \1", c)
    c = c.replace(":Room", " × Room").replace(":Property", " × Property")
    names = {"n_accommodates": "Guests", "n_accommodates2": "Guests squared", "n_beds": "Beds",
             "n_bathrooms": "Bathrooms", "n_days_since": "Days since first review",
             "n_days_since2": "Days since first review, squared"}
    if c in names:
        return names[c]
    if c.startswith("d_"):
        return "Amenity: " + c[2:]
    return c
_coef = pd.Series(lasso.coef_, index=X.columns)
_top = _coef[_coef != 0].abs().sort_values(ascending=False).head(10).index
lasso_top_rows = [{"variable": _nice(c), "coef": round(float(_coef[c]), 2),
                   "sign": "Raises price" if _coef[c] > 0 else "Lowers price"} for c in _top]
m6_cv_rmse = round(air_cv_avg["M6"], 1)
lasso_code_output = (
    ">>> lasso = LassoCV(cv=5).fit(X_scaled, y)\n"
    f">>> lasso.alpha_\n{lasso.alpha_:.3f}\n\n"
    f">>> (lasso.coef_ != 0).sum()   # variables kept out of {n_total}\n{n_nonzero}\n\n"
    f">>> np.sqrt(np.mean((y - lasso.predict(X_scaled))**2))   # in-sample RMSE\n{lasso_rmse:.1f}"
)

# --- Post-selection inference, made concrete: refit LASSO on 30 bootstrap
# resamples of the SAME work set and record how often each of the top-10
# variables from the original fit actually survives. If selection were
# deterministic every row would read 30/30; it isn't.
_n_boot = 30
_boot_rng = np.random.RandomState(7)
_sel_counts = np.zeros(Xs.shape[1])
for _b in range(_n_boot):
    _idx = _boot_rng.choice(len(y), size=len(y), replace=True)
    _lb = LassoCV(cv=5, random_state=_b, max_iter=20000).fit(Xs[_idx], y[_idx])
    _sel_counts += (_lb.coef_ != 0)
_sel_freq = pd.Series(_sel_counts, index=X.columns)
selection_rows = [{"variable": _nice(c), "times": int(_sel_freq[c]), "n_boot": _n_boot} for c in _top]
selection_rows = sorted(selection_rows, key=lambda d: -d["times"])
n_always = sum(1 for d in selection_rows if d["times"] == _n_boot)

# Across ALL candidate variables, not just the top 10: how many are "in"
# every single time, versus how many drift in and out across resamples?
n_always_all = int((_sel_freq == _n_boot).sum())
n_sometimes_all = int(((_sel_freq > 0) & (_sel_freq < _n_boot)).sum())
n_never_all = int((_sel_freq == 0).sum())
n_union_all = int((_sel_freq > 0).sum())

# --- Holdout diagnostics: predicted vs actual on held-out data, best OLS model (M6) ---
# work_df/holdout_df were already split at the very top, before any of the
# model building above — this is the same holdout set, touched for the
# first time only now.
m6_work = smf.ols(air_formulas["M6"], data=work_df).fit()
holdout_pred = m6_work.predict(holdout_df)
holdout_rmse = float(np.sqrt(np.mean((holdout_df["price"] - holdout_pred) ** 2)))

yyhat_data = [
    {"actual": float(a), "predicted": float(p)}
    for a, p in zip(holdout_df["price"], holdout_pred)
    if a < 300 and p < 300
]

ojs_define(
    air_stats_rows       = air_stats_rows,
    air_complexity_data  = air_complexity_data,
    lasso_code_output    = lasso_code_output,
    lasso_top_rows       = lasso_top_rows,
    lasso_rmse           = round(lasso_rmse, 1),
    lasso_cv_rmse        = round(lasso_cv_rmse, 1),
    n_nonzero            = n_nonzero,
    n_total              = n_total,
    m6_cv_rmse           = m6_cv_rmse,
    holdout_rmse         = round(holdout_rmse, 1),
    yyhat_data           = yyhat_data,
    n_work               = n_work,
    n_holdout            = n_holdout,
    sigma_hat            = round(sigma_hat, 3),
    label_actual_mean    = round(label_actual_mean, 1),
    label_naive_mean     = round(label_naive_mean, 1),
    label_corrected_mean = round(label_corrected_mean, 1),
    label_example        = label_example,
    selection_rows       = selection_rows,
    n_boot               = _n_boot,
    n_always             = n_always,
    n_always_all         = n_always_all,
    n_sometimes_all      = n_sometimes_all,
    n_never_all          = n_never_all,
    n_union_all          = n_union_all,
)
```

```{ojs}
{
  // Generic "shrink on reveal" wiring, used by every chart wrapped as
  // `:::: {.shrink-on-reveal data-frag="some-fragment-id" style="--large-height:...;--small-height:...;--shrink-scale:..."}`
  // Each chart renders large while its named fragment is hidden, then
  // shrinks smoothly to make room the moment that fragment is revealed.
  // Sizes live entirely in each wrapper's own inline style — this cell only
  // handles show/hide, once, for every wrapper on the page, so adding a new
  // chart to this pattern never means touching this cell.
  const wrapperFor = (fragId) => document.querySelector(`.shrink-on-reveal[data-frag="${fragId}"]`)

  // Sets each wrapper's correct starting state immediately, including on a
  // reload or direct navigation to a slide whose fragment is already shown
  // — matters because this cell (no reactive deps) only runs once, at load.
  const syncAll = () => {
    document.querySelectorAll('.fragment[id]').forEach(frag =>
      wrapperFor(frag.id)?.classList.toggle('is-small', frag.classList.contains('visible'))
    )
  }
  syncAll()
  // PDF export rebuilds the slide DOM, so re-sync on any change (same fix as Weeks 2, 4, 5 and 6).
  new MutationObserver(syncAll).observe(document.body, { childList: true, subtree: true, attributes: true, attributeFilter: ['class'] })

  Reveal.on('fragmentshown', (event) => {
    wrapperFor(event.fragment.id)?.classList.add('is-small')
  })
  Reveal.on('fragmenthidden', (event) => {
    wrapperFor(event.fragment.id)?.classList.remove('is-small')
  })
}
```

## {background-color="#1a1a2e"}

::: {style="text-align: center; padding-top: 180px;"}
[**Model building for prediction**]{style="font-size: 2.2em; color: white;"}

[The workshop built the toolbox on six clean predictors and 281 cars. This session: what happens with dozens of candidate variables — and 4,393 real Airbnb listings.]{style="font-size: 1.1em; color: #aaa; padding-top: 20px; display: block;"}
:::

---

## Label engineering: choosing the target

Before a single predictor gets chosen, there's a decision about **y** itself. Sometimes the business question settles it outright — the price of the hotel room is the price of the hotel room. Often it genuinely needs deciding: **level, or log?**

- Price is usually closer to a linear relationship with its predictors when expressed in log terms than in levels
- Log differences approximate *percentage* differences, and percentage differences in price are often more stable across very different kinds of listing than pound differences are
- A technical bonus: log prices tend to sit closer to a normal distribution, which helps a linear regression approximate the average relationship well

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:12px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 14
:::

## Converting a log prediction back

Fit `np.log(price) ~ ...` and the model predicts **ln(price)**, not price. Exponentiating the prediction directly undershoots, systematically:

$$\hat y = e^{\widehat{\ln y}} \times e^{\hat\sigma^2/2}$$

::: {.fragment}
Why the extra term: the regression predicts the *average* log price, but we want the average price itself — and because $\ln$ is a curved (concave) function, the average of $e^{\ln y}$ across many listings is **not** the same as $e$ raised to the average $\ln y$. The correction, built from the spread of the regression's own residuals ($\hat\sigma$), puts that back.
:::

::: {.fragment}
```{ojs}
html`<p style="margin:14px 0 4px;">One listing: a ${label_example.accommodates}-guest ${label_example.room_type.toLowerCase()}, actual price <b>£${label_example.actual.toFixed(0)}</b>. Naive: e<sup>${label_example.ln_pred.toFixed(2)}</sup> = <b>£${label_example.naive.toFixed(2)}</b>. Corrected: × e<sup>${sigma_hat.toFixed(3)}²/2</sup> = <b>£${label_example.corrected.toFixed(2)}</b> — closer, though one listing is still just one listing.</p>`
```

```{ojs}
html`<p style="margin:4px 0;">Across all ${n_work.toLocaleString()} work-set listings, the pattern is systematic, not a fluke: actual average price <b>£${label_actual_mean}</b>; naive average prediction <b>£${label_naive_mean}</b> (undershoots by £${(label_actual_mean - label_naive_mean).toFixed(1)}); corrected average prediction <b>£${label_corrected_mean}</b>.</p>`
```
:::

# Feature engineering {background-color="#2d6a4f"}
## Building the right-hand side

---

## What is feature engineering?

- Once the target is settled, feature engineering decides the list of candidate predictors and the functional form each one enters in
- It draws on two things at once: **domain knowledge** — what actually drives price for a short-let listing — and **statistics**, checking which choices the data itself supports
- Gábor & Kézdi call it the most effort-intensive part of building a prediction model, and the part with the biggest payoff

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:12px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 14
:::

## The checklist

1. **Missing values** — random, or systematic? Impute with a flag column, don't just drop the observation
2. **Categorical values** — binary, or a small set of dummies
3. **Text** — mine it for useful signal (a "seminar" keyword, say), otherwise leave it
4. **Functional form** — polynomials, splines, logs — the same choices as the workshop, applied to many variables at once
5. **Interactions** — worth thinking about, expensive to search exhaustively

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:12px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 14
:::

## Real data: Airbnb, London

- 4,393 Hackney-borough listings, March 2017 snapshot
- Target: nightly `price`, in pounds (the textbook labels it dollars, but the listings are in pounds)
- ~70 predictor candidates: capacity, room and property type, cancellation policy, review scores, and 50 individual amenity dummies (`d_tv`, `d_petsallowed`, `d_elevatorinbuilding`, ...)

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:12px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), airbnb dataset, osf.io/qyca8
:::

## Six models, built up by hand

::: {.mid-code}
```{.python}
M1 = smf.ols("price ~ n_accommodates", data=df).fit()
M2 = smf.ols("price ~ n_accommodates + n_beds + C(f_room_type) + C(f_property_type)", data=df).fit()
M3 = smf.ols("price ~ ... + n_bathrooms + C(f_cancellation_policy) + C(f_bed_type)", data=df).fit()
M4 = smf.ols("price ~ ... + n_accommodates2 + n_days_since + n_days_since2", data=df).fit()
M5 = smf.ols("price ~ ... + C(f_room_type)*C(f_property_type)", data=df).fit()
M6 = smf.ols("price ~ ... + " + " + ".join(amenity_dummies), data=df).fit()  # 50 amenities
```
:::

Each step adds more: capacity and type, then physical features, then non-linearity and interactions, then every amenity.

## Comparing the six models

```{ojs}
{
  const cols = ["Model", "N coef", "R2", "Training RMSE", "CV RMSE", "BIC"];
  return html`<table style="margin:20px auto 0;font-family:sans-serif;font-size:0.85em;border-collapse:collapse;">
    <tr style="border-bottom:2px solid #1a1a2e;">${cols.map(c => `<th style="padding:5px 14px;text-align:center;">${c}</th>`).join('')}</tr>
    ${air_stats_rows.map(d => `<tr style="border-bottom:1px solid #ddd;">${cols.map(c => `<td style="padding:4px 14px;text-align:center;">${d[c]}</td>`).join('')}</tr>`).join('')}
  </table>`
}
```

::: {.fragment}
RMSE keeps improving all the way to M6, but the **BIC** column is lowest at M4 and rises again for M6: it penalises M6's 65 coefficients even where cross-validated RMSE doesn't. Different criteria, different sensitivity to complexity.
:::

---

# Selecting variables automatically {background-color="#2d6a4f"}
## LASSO

---

## We can't try every model

- Each candidate predictor is either in or out, so $p$ candidates give $2^p$ possible models. With 70 candidates that's more than $10^{21}$: far too many to try
- **By hand**: domain knowledge drives the choice — interpretable, but slow, and impossible with many interactions
- **By algorithm**: let the data suggest which variables earn their place

## Building a model by hand

Even when an algorithm does the final selection, the groundwork is still done by hand:

- Domain knowledge picks the key variables first — what plausibly drives price for a short-let listing, before any statistic gets consulted
- Drop the garbage: comb through candidates and cut the ones with poor coverage, poor quality, or no plausible relevance
- Check pairwise correlations — multicollinearity bites harder the smaller the dataset
- Prefer variables that are cheap to keep updating — a model running in production has to be fed, not just fitted once
- How far this can go depends on the ratio of variables to observations, not the raw count of either on its own

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:12px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 14
:::

## What LASSO does

- LASSO — Least Absolute Shrinkage and Selection Operator — picks variables to include in a regression automatically, built to produce good predictions and avoid overfitting
- It's a **shrinkage method**: every coefficient gets pulled towards zero, which reduces variance
- It's also a **feature-selection method**: some coefficients get pulled all the way to exactly zero, dropping that variable from the model entirely
- Both happen at once, inside the same single fitting step — no separate "shrink" and "select" stages

## The LASSO equation

LASSO adds a penalty to the usual OLS minimisation:

$$\min_\beta \left\{ \sum_{i=1}^{N}\left(y_i - \beta_0 - \sum_{j=1}^{k}\beta_j x_{ij}\right)^2 + \lambda\sum_{j=1}^{k}|\beta_j| \right\}$$

::: {.fragment}
- The first term is the familiar OLS objective: fit the data as closely as possible
- The second is new: a penalty proportional to the **sum of the absolute values** of the coefficients
- $\lambda$ sets how much that penalty weighs against fit. $\lambda = 0$ gives plain OLS back; larger $\lambda$ pulls harder, and more variables drop out
:::

## Side note: LASSO vs. BIC

Both exist to balance fit against complexity — the same goal as the BIC column two slides ago — but they get there differently:

- **BIC** scores a model *after* it's been fitted, so you can compare several separately-built candidates and pick the one with the best in-sample measure of fit
- **LASSO** doesn't produce a score to compare models with. It alters the coefficients *during* fitting, so the penalty is already built into the one model it hands you

::: {style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:12px;"}
Source: Békés & Kézdi (2021), Ch. 14
:::

## Why some coefficients hit exactly zero {.smaller}

Every coefficient faces a trade: a bigger $\beta_j$ may fit the data a little better, but it costs more penalty. Where that trade settles depends on *how the penalty's pull changes as $\beta_j$ shrinks* — and that's where LASSO and ridge genuinely differ.

```{ojs}
Plot.plot({
  width: 700, height: 230, marginLeft: 50,
  x: {label: "Coefficient β"}, y: {label: "Penalty"},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["LASSO: λ|β|", "Ridge: λβ²"], range: ["#2c3e7a", "#c0392b"]},
  marks: [
    Plot.line(d3.range(-2, 2.01, 0.05).map(b => ({b, p: Math.abs(b), k: "LASSO: λ|β|"})), {x: "b", y: "p", stroke: "k", strokeWidth: 2.5}),
    Plot.line(d3.range(-2, 2.01, 0.05).map(b => ({b, p: b * b / 2, k: "Ridge: λβ²"})), {x: "b", y: "p", stroke: "k", strokeWidth: 2.5}),
    Plot.ruleX([0], {stroke: "#999"})
  ]
})
```

::: {.fragment}
- **LASSO's penalty (blue) is a straight line through zero.** Its slope — the saving from nudging $\beta_j$ a little closer to zero — is exactly the same whether $\beta_j$ is large or already tiny. That constant pull never lets up, so the moment a variable's contribution to fit drops below it, the best move is to push all the way to zero, not just partway
- **Ridge's penalty (red) is a curve that flattens near zero.** Its slope shrinks right along with $\beta_j$, so the closer you get to zero, the weaker the incentive to go any further. Coefficients get small, but the pull fades out before they ever actually reach it
:::

## The cost: bias

- OLS is unbiased. LASSO isn't — that's the trade it makes for lower variance
- Unlike OLS, there's no closed-form solution; an algorithm solves for $\beta$ and $\lambda$ together
- $\lambda$ itself is chosen by cross-validation: try many values, pick the one with the best CV RMSE

::: {.fragment}
The two penalty shapes have names: LASSO's is "L1," ridge's squared penalty is "L2." Regularisation covers both.
:::

## LASSO on the Airbnb data

::: {.mid-code}
```{.python}
from sklearn.linear_model import LassoCV
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

X_scaled = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)   # LASSO needs standardised features
lasso = LassoCV(cv=5).fit(X_scaled, y)
```
:::

```{ojs}
html`<pre style="font-family:'SF Mono','Menlo',monospace;font-size:0.68em;line-height:1.4;
                  background:#f6f6f8;border:1px solid #e0e0e6;border-radius:6px;
                  padding:8px 14px;overflow-x:auto;white-space:pre;">${lasso_code_output}</pre>`
```

```{ojs}
html`<div class="instructions-box">LASSO kept ${n_nonzero} of ${n_total} candidate coefficients, chosen automatically. Its cross-validated RMSE (${lasso_cv_rmse.toFixed(1)}) matches M6's OLS fit (${m6_cv_rmse.toFixed(1)}) with fewer moving parts.</div>`
```

## What survived

```{ojs}
Plot.plot({
  width: 1000, height: 430, marginLeft: 300,
  x: {label: "Coefficient on standardised variable (£ per night, per standard deviation)", grid: true},
  y: {label: null, domain: lasso_top_rows.map(d => d.variable)},
  color: {legend: true, domain: ["Raises price", "Lowers price"], range: ["#2d6a4f", "#c0392b"]},
  marks: [
    Plot.barX(lasso_top_rows, {x: "coef", y: "variable", fill: "sign"}),
    Plot.ruleX([0])
  ]
```

The ten largest of the coefficients LASSO kept. Size and room type dominate, but several individual amenities survive the penalty too.

## Why classical inference fails after LASSO {.smaller}

LASSO gives coefficients but no standard errors or p-values — and that's not an oversight, it's unavoidable. Two separate things are going on:

- **Which variables survive is itself decided by the data.** LASSO's selection step and its coefficient estimates come from the *same* sample. Classical standard errors and p-values are built on the assumption that the model was fixed on paper before any data arrived — here, it wasn't
- **So applied after LASSO, they understate the real uncertainty.** This is called **post-selection inference**, and it doesn't go away if you refit plain OLS on just the survivors and read *that* model's p-values — the variables going in were still chosen by looking at this data first

::: {.fragment}
Here's the counterfactual a classical SE formula actually relies on: *if we reran this exact study on a fresh sample, would we get the same model back?* For OLS, where the variable list is fixed in advance, only the coefficients would move — that's all the formula has to account for. For LASSO, the variable *list itself* would likely come back different too, since which coefficients survive depends on this sample's own noise. A formula built to describe only the first kind of wobble can't speak to the second — the next slide makes that second kind of wobble visible, not just claimed.
:::

## The selection step, made visible {.smaller}

Refit LASSO on **${n_boot} different bootstrap resamples** of the exact same work set — same ${n_work.toLocaleString()} listings, resampled with replacement each time.

```{ojs}
html`<p>Every one of the <b>${n_union_all}</b> candidate variables got selected at least once somewhere across the ${n_boot} resamples. Only <b>${n_always_all}</b> were selected every single time; the other <b>${n_sometimes_all}</b> came and went — including, on a smaller scale, ${10 - n_always} of the 10 variables the original single fit leaned on hardest:</p>`
```

::: {.fragment}
```{ojs}
{
  const cols = ["Variable", "Selected (of 30 resamples)"];
  return html`<table style="margin:8px auto 0;font-family:sans-serif;font-size:0.72em;border-collapse:collapse;">
    <tr style="border-bottom:2px solid #1a1a2e;">${cols.map(c => `<th style="padding:3px 16px;text-align:left;">${c}</th>`).join('')}</tr>
    ${selection_rows.map(d => `<tr style="border-bottom:1px solid #ddd;"><td style="padding:3px 16px;">${d.variable}</td><td style="padding:3px 16px;">${d.times} / ${d.n_boot}</td></tr>`).join('')}
  </table>`
}
```
:::

## Why LASSO is still reasonable

- That's fine for prediction: we judge the model on held-out RMSE, not on any one coefficient's p-value
- LASSO accepts a little bias for a lot less variance — exactly the right trade when the goal is predicting new cases, not estimating one specific effect
- For a causal question (Week 9), choose the controls by reasoning about the diagram, not by letting LASSO pick them. LASSO is a prediction tool, not an inference tool

# Post-prediction diagnostics {background-color="#2d6a4f"}
## Holdout sets

---

## One more split before you trust the number

- Model selection (BIC, cross-validation) already uses the data — repeatedly
- Best practice: carve off a **holdout set** right at the start, and don't touch it until the very end
- **Work set**: model building, model selection, training/test folds — all happen here
- **Holdout set**: touched exactly once, to get an honest read on how the chosen model will do on genuinely new data

## The workflow

1. Split the original data into a work set and a holdout set
2. Inside the work set: training/test folds, k-fold CV, model selection
3. Re-estimate the winning model on the *whole* work set
4. Apply it to the holdout set — untouched until now
5. Evaluate: this is the honest estimate of live-data performance

```{ojs}
html`<p style="font-size:0.75em;color:#999;margin-top:14px;">Steps 1 and 2 already happened: the ${n_work.toLocaleString()}/${n_holdout.toLocaleString()} split came first, before any model got built, and every model above — the comparison table, every cross-validation fold, the LASSO fit and its bootstrap resamples — came from the work set alone.</p>`
```

## Step 3: choosing the winning model {.smaller}

Model selection didn't actually hand us one clear winner — it handed us a trade-off, back on "Comparing the six models":

```{ojs}
{
  const m4 = air_stats_rows.find(d => d.Model === "M4"), m6 = air_stats_rows.find(d => d.Model === "M6");
  return html`<table style="margin:10px auto 0;font-family:sans-serif;font-size:0.85em;border-collapse:collapse;">
    <tr style="border-bottom:2px solid #1a1a2e;"><th style="padding:5px 16px;"></th><th style="padding:5px 16px;">N coef</th><th style="padding:5px 16px;">CV RMSE</th><th style="padding:5px 16px;">BIC</th></tr>
    <tr style="border-bottom:1px solid #ddd;"><td style="padding:4px 16px;"><b>M4</b> — BIC's pick</td><td style="padding:4px 16px;text-align:center;">${m4["N coef"]}</td><td style="padding:4px 16px;text-align:center;">${m4["CV RMSE"]}</td><td style="padding:4px 16px;text-align:center;"><b>${m4.BIC.toLocaleString()}</b></td></tr>
    <tr><td style="padding:4px 16px;"><b>M6</b> — lowest CV RMSE</td><td style="padding:4px 16px;text-align:center;">${m6["N coef"]}</td><td style="padding:4px 16px;text-align:center;"><b>${m6["CV RMSE"]}</b></td><td style="padding:4px 16px;text-align:center;">${m6.BIC.toLocaleString()}</td></tr>
  </table>`
}
```

::: {.fragment}
M6's CV RMSE beats M4's by about £1, at the cost of 52 extra coefficients — and BIC, which penalises exactly that, prefers M4 by a wide margin (36,038 against 36,184). Neither answer is wrong; they're optimising different things. **This session's call: M6**, because the stated goal is predicting price as accurately as possible, and the extra accuracy — however small — is the thing actually being asked for. A project valuing a simpler, cheaper-to-maintain model would reasonably choose M4 instead, and should say so explicitly rather than let the software's default choice decide quietly.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Step 3 itself: M6 gets **re-estimated on the whole work set** — not a training fold, not the held-back 20% — exactly the `m6_work` fit already used below.
:::

## Summary

- Prediction with many candidate variables needs the same discipline as prediction with a few — just automated where hand-picking becomes infeasible
- Log targets need a correction term before converting back — skipping it silently biases predictions down
- LASSO trades a little bias for a lot less variance, and sets weak coefficients to exactly zero. It gives no valid p-values, so use it for prediction, not inference
- A holdout set, touched only once, is the honest final check — everything before it is negotiable, this isn't
